text:
Utah built a 5-2 lead by the 19th minute of the second period, and Toronto spent the rest of the night proving it should never have been that wide. The Maple Leafs finished with 3.01 expected goals to Utah's 2.45 and would win about 60 percent of simulated replays of every shot, yet Daniil But, Vincent Trocheck, Mikhail Sergachev, Dylan Guenther and MacKenzie Weegar all scored before Toronto could close the gap. The Leafs' last push fell one goal short, 5-4.

The shape of the game explains the gap. At even strength Utah held a clear edge in chance quality, 2.03 expected goals to 1.10, so the Leafs' advantage came almost entirely from the power play, where they went 2 for 5 with goals from Auston Matthews and John Tavares. Utah also cashed in on low-percentage looks: Sergachev's shorthanded wrist shot had about a 2 percent chance of going in, and Guenther's snap shot was the same. Two of those cheap goals came in the span of ten minutes in the second period.

Goaltending tilted the night further. Anthony Stolarz allowed five goals on 2.45 expected, about two and a half goals worse than the shots called for, while Karel Vejmelka gave up four against 3.01 expected. Toronto's third period was its best stretch, 1.16 expected goals to Utah's 0.73, and Tavares and Gavin McKenna scored to make it 5-4, but the clock ran out first. Matthews (1.1 expected goals on his own shots at ice level) and Sergachev, first star with a goal and an assist, both left their mark.
